title: Board repair, gaps and stop-and-refer conditions
audience: Timber floor restoration workers who assess and repair surface defects in timber boards within an approved scope.
learningOutcomes: Classify each board defect as cosmetic, structural or suspect before any repair.
Carry out approved cosmetic repairs to gaps and small surface defects within scope.
Stop and refer structural, water-related, rot, insect or hazardous-material defects.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: SafeWork SA, Asbestos licences: Class A, Class B and assessor licence (no date shown); WorkSafe Victoria, Wood dust: health hazards and control (reviewed 17 April 2026).

instruction.heading: Classify every defect first
instruction.body: Every defect is recorded as cosmetic, structural or suspect before any repair. A cosmetic defect is a surface mark, a small gap or a minor chip that the approved scope covers. A structural defect is one that affects the strength or movement of the floor, such as a bouncing or sagging board, a rotten or crushed board, or movement that suggests a joist or subfloor problem. A suspect defect is one where the cause is not clear, such as a dark stain that may be water, insect damage, or a glued joint that may contain hazardous material.

instruction.heading: Structural and water-related defects are referred
instruction.body: Structural repair, subfloor work and any decision that a floor is structurally sound are outside this course. A bouncing board or sag must be referred to a qualified person. A dark stain that may come from water is referred, because the cause must be found before it is filled or finished. Filling a stain or a soft board to make it look better hides a problem that the next owner will inherit. Record the referral with photos and the location.

instruction.heading: Cosmetic repairs within scope
instruction.body: Where the scope allows, small gaps and surface chips can be filled with a filler approved for the timber and the finish. Test the filler colour on an offcut or an inconspicuous area first. Fill after the screening stage, not before, so that the filler is not sanded out or pulled from the joint. Allow the filler to cure as the manufacturer states, and sand it flush with the surrounding surface. Sanding filler creates dust, so the same extraction and HEPA controls for wood dust apply.

instruction.heading: Loose boards
instruction.body: A loose board that moves under foot may point to a fixing or joist problem. Refix a board only by the method stated in the approved scope. Where the cause of the movement is not clear, treat the board as structural and refer it. Do not add screws or adhesive to a board you have not classified.

instruction.heading: Suspect adhesive and material
instruction.body: A joint or edge that shows adhesive, black mastic or old filler may contain hazardous material. Stop and assess it under “Pre-start assessment: lead, asbestos and suspect materials in old floors” before any cutting, grinding or filling. Do not fill over a suspect adhesive joint, because the filler does not change the hazard and the disturbance may release dust.

procedure: Map every defect on the floor plan and classify it as cosmetic, structural or suspect.
Refer any structural, water-related, rot, insect or subfloor defect, and record the referral.
Stop and assess any suspect adhesive or material before disturbing it.
For cosmetic defects only, test the approved filler on an offcut and record the colour check.
Fill gaps after screening, allow the filler to cure, and sand it flush with the surface.
Re-check each repaired area under raking light, and record the repair and any remaining defects.

workedExamples.situation: In a hallway, one board bounces when walked on. A dark stain sits near the bathroom door. The client asks you to fill the stain so the floor looks even for the sale.
workedExamples.reasoning: The bounce suggests a structural or fixing problem that is outside the course. The dark stain near a bathroom may come from water, so its cause must be found before it is filled. Refer both, record them with photos and location, and do not fill the stain as if it were fixed. Tell the client in writing what has been referred and what the course does not cover.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved timber filler in a colour matched on an offcut
Fixing tools for the approved method only
Photo record and floor plan for the defect map
Extraction and respiratory protection for sanding filler (see “Dust control: extraction, wet cleaning and safe clean-up” and “Respiratory protection and fit: the last layer of control”)

commonErrors.error: Filling a stain without finding its cause.
commonErrors.prevention: Classify the stain as suspect and refer it before any filling.

commonErrors.error: Treating a bouncing board as a cosmetic defect.
commonErrors.prevention: Classify movement as structural and refer it.

commonErrors.error: Filling over a suspect adhesive joint without assessment.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop and assess under “Pre-start assessment: lead, asbestos and suspect materials in old floors” first.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Structural, subfloor and water-related defects are outside this course. Refer them to a qualified person.

Suspect adhesive or material may contain asbestos or lead. In South Australia, SafeWork SA's licence page (no date shown) describes Class A and Class B removal licences. Follow “Pre-start assessment: lead, asbestos and suspect materials in old floors” before any disturbance.

qualityStandard: Every defect is recorded as cosmetic, structural or suspect before any repair.
No structural, subfloor or water-related defect is repaired under this course.
Filler colour is checked on an offcut and the repaired area is checked under raking light.
documentationEvidence: Defect map with photos and classification for each defect
Referral record for structural, water-related or suspect defects
Repair record for cosmetic work, with filler and colour check
summary: Classify every defect as cosmetic, structural or suspect before repairing.
Refer structural, water-related and suspect defects. Do not hide them with filler.
Fill only cosmetic defects within scope, after screening, and check the result.
referencesAtEnd: Official sources to recheck before any job: SafeWork SA, Asbestos licences: Class A, Class B and assessor licence (no date shown); WorkSafe Victoria, Wood dust: health hazards and control (reviewed 17 April 2026).

knowledgeChecks.question: A board bounces and a dark stain sits near a bathroom door. What is correct?
options: Fill the stain and finish the floor on the day
Sand harder over the stain to lift it out fast
Refer the structural or water concern and record it
Cover it with a rug to hide it from the client

knowledgeChecks.question: Which defect is cosmetic within this course?
options: Subfloor sag under the living room, the hall, the stairs and the entry
Rot in a joist below the floor near the wall, door and the stair
Water damage with a soft board in the room near the door and wall
A small surface gap that the approved scope allows you to fill

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should filler be tested on an offcut first?
options: To check the colour and the finish
To heat the floor boards up first
To avoid sanding the floor entirely
To set the price of the job early

knowledgeChecks.question: What must happen when a suspect adhesive joint is found?
options: Fill it and continue with the floor
Stop and assess it before disturbing it
Cut it out with a grinder on site
Ignore it because it is old and stable

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is sanding filler a dust issue?
options: It has no dust at all on the job or the floor
It only affects the paint on the walls
It creates airborne dust that needs extraction
It removes the wood from the floor surface
